planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or plugs after frost danger has passed; roots overwinter outdoors in zones 6-9 but top growth is killed by hard frost elsewhere, so most gardeners treat it as a basket or container annual.

directions: This selection forms a low trailing mat of glossy foliage topped with dense clusters of bright yellow flowers through spring and summer, making it a dependable spiller for hanging baskets, window boxes, and mixed containers. It tolerates both heat and shade better than many trailing bedding plants, so it keeps performing even in a basket that gets uneven light through the day. Grow in humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist but drains well, and feed lightly since it does not need heavy fertilizing to fill out. Where winters stay above roughly -10F the crown can survive to resprout the following spring.

planting.note: Set out nursery transplants in spring or early fall; this interspecific Sweet William reliably overwinters to USDA zone 5 and reblooms for multiple seasons rather than behaving as a biennial.

directions: Pink Magic joins the Rockin' line of interspecific Sweet Williams with vivid pink single flowers carried on upright stems well above the foliage, and it keeps producing bloom flushes from early spring into winter in milder climates. Unlike old-fashioned biennial Sweet William, this hybrid comes back reliably year after year once established in a sunny or lightly shaded border. The clove-scented flowers draw bees and butterflies, and plants hold up well without staking. Feed every couple of weeks during active growth and deadhead spent spikes to encourage the next flush.

planting.note: Set out transplants in spring once soil is workable; this compact English lavender flowers earlier than many angustifolia selections and prefers lean, well-drained soil.

directions: This compact English lavender produces a tight, well-branched mound of silvery foliage and opens its fragrant blue flower spikes earlier in the season than many other angustifolia types, extending the lavender display. It needs lean, light to moderately fertile soil with sharp drainage and resents being overwatered or overfed. Shear the whole plant back lightly in early spring before new growth starts to keep it dense and prevent the woody base from opening up over time. Its small size and drought tolerance suit it well to rock gardens, edging, and containers where heavier lavenders would sprawl.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in darkness ahead of the cool season, or set out nursery plugs for fall color; blooms continuously through cool weather and can hold winter interest in milder zones.

directions: Harvest Moon covers itself in fragrant golden-yellow blooms over dark green foliage, with a mounded and trailing habit that spreads wider than most viola cultivars, making it useful for spilling over container rims as well as filling garden beds. It holds up to both summer heat and light shade better than many cool-season violas, and frost only slows rather than stops flowering. Keep soil enriched with compost and evenly moist, and feed every couple of weeks to sustain the long bloom run from early spring into autumn. In milder climates it can carry color through much of the winter.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in darkness eight to ten weeks before setting out for spring color, or plant in fall where pansies overwinter; extra-large flowers form on sturdy stems that resist flopping.

directions: This Matrix series selection produces extra-large white flowers marked with a central blotch, carried on strong, sturdy stems that pack more blooms per plant than typical pansy types. Its mounded, uniform habit makes it reliable for mass bedding as well as containers, and the flowers attract bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Plant in early spring or fall for the best flowering window, since the series tolerates both frost and cool temperatures but slows in summer heat. Fertilize every couple of weeks and deadhead if plants start to look ragged to keep fresh buds coming.

planting.note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed; Serena Rose adds a rose-pink option to the compact, seed-grown Serena breeding line alongside the blue, white, and purple colors already in commerce.

directions: Serena Rose carries spikes of rose-pink, snapdragon-like flowers on a columnar, well-branched plant that needs no pinching to stay full and tidy. It is sold as a low-maintenance, drought- and heat-tolerant choice for beds and mixed containers, shrugging off the kind of sustained summer heat that stalls true snapdragons. Avoid letting the root zone dry out completely between waterings even though established plants tolerate some drought, and feed every couple of weeks to keep the continuous bloom cycle going from late spring through late summer. Deer and rabbits generally leave it alone.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in darkness eight to ten weeks before setting out for spring color, or plant in fall; Panola XP Yellow fills out the multiflora Panola XP series alongside picotee colors already in commerce.

directions: This multiflora selection covers itself in clear yellow flowers with thicker-than-average petals that shrug off winter weather better than thinner-petaled pansies. Its compact, mounded habit makes it a dependable choice for mass bedding, borders, and containers where consistent color is the goal rather than oversized individual blooms. Plant in early spring or in fall where pansies overwinter, since fall-set plants often rebloom reliably the following spring. Feed every couple of weeks through the bloom season and expect steady flowering from early spring through autumn, slowing only in summer heat.
